paras: The lynching of Bill Harris was the shooting of a Black man by a pursuing mob at his wife's house in Bastrop parish, Louisiana, around November 1, 1882. Harris was accused of attacking the young daughter of a white planter named Wilder, and the party that captured him fired twenty guns at him at once. The story reached papers across the country through a Shreveport wire dispatch under headlines such as "Twenty Shots at One Man."

According to a dispatch datelined Shreveport, November 1, Harris, described as "a negro," attacked a little girl, the daughter of George L. Wilder, "a white planter of Bastrop parish," the previous evening. Shorter versions said he "attempted to outrage" the child, while weekly roundups called it a "brutal assault" or said he "grossly assaulted" her. One account placed the episode "near Bastrop, Moorehouse Parish."

Several people were said to have witnessed the act and raised an alarm, and Harris fled. A "large party of citizens" pursued him and captured him at the residence of his wife. Twenty guns were then fired at him simultaneously, and in the dispatch's words "his head was blown from his body."
The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer's version said he was captured "this morning," while the Bismarck Tribune, under a November 2 dateline, said the crowd found him "last night."
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the papers named anyone in the party that killed Harris.

Every surviving account derives from the Shreveport dispatch, which reached northern and western papers within days. The Daily Gazette ran it on November 1 as a two-sentence brief among other telegrams, and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer printed the fuller text the next day as "Twenty Shots at One Man." The Bismarck Tribune headed its version "They Shot His Head Off," and the Somerset Herald reprinted the full dispatch on November 8.

Weekly roundups in Minnesota and Ohio reduced the story to a single line among fires and murders; the Mower County Transcript said Harris was "run down by a posse of citizens who riddled him with bullets." All of these papers treated the accusation as established fact and called the killers "citizens" or "a mob" without comment on the killing itself.
The planter's name appears as George Wilder, George D. Wilder, George L. Wilder and J. H. Wilder, variants that likely reflect telegraph and typesetting errors in a single dispatch.

accounts.label: Shreveport wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Harris attacked Wilder's little girl, was seen and fled; a large party of citizens pursued and captured him at his wife's residence, where twenty guns were fired at him at once.

accounts.label: Condensed wire brief
accounts.gist: Harris attempted to outrage Wilder's daughter; a mob pursued him and he was shot and killed.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Twenty Shots at One Man' and 'They Shot His Head Off' dwell on the gunfire; the accusation is given as fact and the killers are called 'citizens' without comment.
Ran as one line in brief-telegram columns and weekly crime roundups beside unrelated murders and fires.

conflicts.note: A4 carries a Nov. 2 dateline, so 'last night' may mean the night of Nov. 1; A7 says the attack was 'last evening' in a Nov. 1 dispatch.

Wording of the accusation varies across condensations of one dispatch.
